Wait, you've never heard of buying out apartments? Like, what? I genuinely don't understand how you could possibly not know that apartment/floor ownership is a thing.

Well. It works like this: instead of paying rent every month to the owner of the apartment, you own the apartment and only pay things like water and electricity. And possibly rent out the apartment to someone else. The same logic applies to owning floors of a large buildings. The real-estate development companies that buy up condemned buildings, demolish them and then build new ones can make a good profit from just selling out the building piece-by-piece, instead of trying to find a buyer that can afford to buy the whole building at once. Selling out buildings like that makes up for costs incurred to build the building in the first place, as well as a profit to present to the investors. It also keeps them out of the big hassle and paper-pushing that is being in the business of renting real-estate out to tenants. While renting it out would be more profitable in the long term, it's an entirely different business compared to construction and development, and companies focused on architecture and development may not want to get into something as slow-paced as that. It's very, very expensive to keep an architect on salary without having anything productive for them to do, and you don't want to lose that kind of talent to other companies. Thus RE development companies do need to cash out relatively quickly to have the funds to start new projects and keep their talented employees working.
